name: albanian_05
context: A Facebook comment under a post by the National Institute of Public Health of Kosovo during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The comment is in Albanian, mostly the informal Kosovo (Gheg) dialect, often written without the letters ë and ç.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 0 badly over-predicts negative: 172 of 345 neutral texts went to negative, while negative recall is already high. These annotators use neutral very broadly. It covers complaints, policy criticism, doubts about the numbers, arithmetic corrections, worry about rising cases, ironic jokes, laughter, tags and town-league banter. Negative needs open hostility: direct charges of lying or fraud, insults, or partisan jabs. Positive also includes caring advice to stay safe, 'perhajr' greetings, sincere hope and 'Rip covid'. Jokey 'ishalla' and plain notes that numbers fell stay neutral. I have trimmed the wording to fit the 400-word limit.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 1 overcorrected. Neutral is now well recognised (310/345), but negative recall fell from 144 to 58, with 96 negatives called neutral. The missed negatives share a frustrated, distrustful or alarmed tone even without insults. Examples are hints that figures are fake or copy-pasted ('copy paste', 'diçka nuk është në rregull', 'a ju besohet', 'Garant me 1 shurr'), sarcastic 'situata nën kontroll', angry demands ('futja karantine', 'qitni masat se nau qi nana'), alarm or despair ('Tmerr', 'KEQ!!!', 'ka me u ba shume keq'), contemptuous blame of the public or government, and mask or virus denial ('Maska = skllavëri'). The neutrals that version 0 wrongly called negative were calmer: arithmetic corrections, puzzled questions, constructive policy suggestions, playful banter between tagged friends, town-ranking jokes, and mild 'sa keq'. So the line should be tone: calm, playful or constructive means neutral, while suspicious, exasperated, scornful or alarmed means negative. Positive misses are mostly relieved notes that numbers are falling ('Lakorja paska fillu me ra', 'E pasni zbut pak sot'). I will make falling numbers positive. False positives come from jokey 'ishalla' and from greetings or mask reminders to tagged friends; I will keep those neutral.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 2 swung too far to negative. Neutral recall collapsed to 120/345 because calm questions, ranking banter, suggestions, jokes and mild worry were all read as negative. Version 1 had the best balance (F1 69.5) but missed negatives that are openly distrustful or exasperated without insults. So I will return to version 1's neutral-by-default framing and widen negative only for clear, strong markers. The first is an explicit claim that figures are faked, copied or manipulated ('copy paste', 'prapaskena', 'Garant me 1 shurr', 'jeni tu mshef raste'). The second is a sarcastic 'situata nën kontroll'. The third is swearing ('nanen', 'qi nana'). The fourth is strong emotional exclamations ('Tmerr', 'KEQ!!!', 'marre', 'na lodhet', 'bollni ma'). The fifth is calls for resignation and denial slogans ('Maska = skllavëri'). Plain questions, arithmetic corrections, calm doubts ('a bash krejt...?'), dry irony about testing, policy demands, town-league jokes and tags stay neutral. For positive, falling-number remarks were inconsistent and the shift in version 2 did not help, so I am keeping version 1's positive definition.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 4 dropped to 74.4 because adding 'relief that cases are falling' to positive pulled 38 neutrals into positive. These were plain or joking notes about lower numbers, 'ishalla' wishes, prayers, town banter and greetings. It gained only 6 positives. Its negative tweaks (short suspicion, partisan jabs) changed little. I will return to version 3, the best so far at 77.6, and keep only the low-risk additions from version 4. The first is the explicit statement that teasing of tagged friends and reasoned critiques are neutral. The second is the party-card and 'dyshimt' examples for negative. Positive goes back to warmth, thanks, praise, blessings and caring advice. Notes that cases fell, including hopeful ones, are explicitly neutral unless they contain clear praise or blessing. I am also restoring version 3's question wording, without 'relief'.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 5 (76.0) scored below version 3 (77.6). Two of its changes hurt. The 'Paska ra pak pi dje' neutral example and the rule that notes about falling cases are neutral cost positive recall: relieved remarks like 'Lakorja paska fillu me ra' and 'E pasni zbut pak sot' went to neutral. The 'dyshimt' cue also misfired on 'raste te dyshimta' ('suspected cases'), and neutral→negative rose to 62. Version 4 showed that pushing falling numbers into positive overshoots, so the best course is to leave falling-number remarks unaddressed and let the model judge tone, as version 3 did. I will restore version 3 almost exactly. The only addition is 'teasing of tagged friends' in the neutral rule, which is low-risk, to cover tagged-friend jokes like 'ti po mshefesh' and 'nale doren'. I am dropping 'dyshimt' and the party-card example. The many remaining errors look like annotator noise and are hard to fix without trade-offs.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 7 (76.3) raised positive recall to 81/96 with the 'Lakorja paska fillu me ra' example, but neutral→negative rose to 68. Some neutrals also went to positive ('Paska ra pak pi dje', prayers). Across versions 3 to 7 the scores sit within about 1.5 points, so the variation is largely noise. The biggest error bucket remains neutral→negative: long indignant critiques, ironic remarks about testing, gloomy predictions, and town banter. I will go back to version 3's wording, the best at 77.6, and keep the 'Lakorja' positive example, which earned positive recall. I will also add a tie-break: when unsure between neutral and negative, choose neutral. Neutral is more than twice as frequent as negative, and the model's negative precision (about 65%) is lower than its recall (about 74%), so a mild shift toward neutral should help. 'Relief' in positive stays limited to the example, without a rule-level push.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 8 (77.1) behaves like versions 3 and 6. The tie-break toward neutral cut neutral→negative to 49 but raised negative→neutral to 45, so the net effect was neutral. The scores have plateaued around 77, and most remaining errors are idiosyncratic (sarcasm only an annotator would read as negative, or tagged-friend jokes read as hostile). One consistent gap is negatives with explicit swearing, partisan jabs or insults that the model still calls neutral: 'Nau Qi Nana', 'nanen jav qifsha', 'libreze partie', 'per interesa tjuve', 'budall'. These are low-risk to add because such markers rarely appear in neutral texts. I will drop the blanket tie-break, which mostly shuffled errors, and replace it with a softer statement that negative needs one of the listed markers. I will also swap the obvious 'Rrenaa' example for the party-card example and add swearing and party cues. Positive and neutral stay as in version 8.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 9 (77.2) recovered negative recall (121/159) by adding swearing and partisan cues, but neutral→negative rose to 66. Version 8's blanket tie-break had the opposite effect. Many of version 9's neutral→negative errors fall into two recognisable groups. The first is long, reasoned complaints about policy, testing or public behaviour (Mitrovica mosques, Ferizaj doctor, the government's curfew logic, the testing-shortage post). The second is teasing aimed at tagged friends rather than officials ('Etrit Sinani ti po mshefesh', 'O nale doren izet', 'Lirim R. Ferizaj bro'). For the final version I keep version 9's negative markers and add a targeted neutral statement covering these two groups, instead of a general tie-break. That should cut neutral→negative without losing the short, explicit negatives. I trim the 'what' fields to stay under 400 words.
